slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1900 and 1910 censuses interpolated to November 1908; men 21+ outside the eleven Southern states (including declarant aliens where they could vote); turnout and choice from the backbone, calibrated to certified 1908 returns.

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: 1900 and 1910 censuses interpolated to November 1908; women 21+ outside the South; women could vote for president only in Wyoming, Colorado (1893), Utah and Idaho (1896).

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1900 and 1910 censuses interpolated to November 1908; white adults in the eleven former Confederate states (includes a small number of American Indian and Asian adults); calibrated to certified 1908 returns.

slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1900 and 1910 censuses interpolated to November 1908; Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; disfranchisement was near complete across the region (Georgia's October 1908 amendment joined the poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses already in force); the shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion.

slices.label: Immigrants not yet citizens
slices.source: 1900 and 1910 censuses interpolated to November 1908; foreign-born white adults who were aliens or had only declared their intent (first papers); declarant aliens could vote in several Midwestern and Western states (fewer each decade as states repealed it), so part of this slice could vote.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1908 comes out as it did: Taft wins, 321–162. The closest state was Missouri, which went to Taft by 0.1 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1900 and 1910 census counts interpolated to 1908 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1908 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: I wish I could have my say tomorrow, but the law doesn't permit women to vote in this state. My husband will cast our family's ballot.
south-white.controlQuote: I wish I could have my say tomorrow, but the law doesn't permit women to vote in this state. My husband will cast our family's ballot.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: I cannot vote—women aren't allowed to in New York. My husband will cast our household's ballot tomorrow.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: The tariff keeps my mill going and wages steady. I'll vote for the administration's man tomorrow, though I've heard the other side has a point about the trusts.
